structure.title: Preamble and clauses 1–11 · The opening grants · Who inherits what?
structure.text: The king confirms liberties of the Church before moving into the costly business of inheriting land. Payments due from heirs, the handling of a ward's property and the position of a widow occupy clauses that might surprise a reader expecting the charter to begin with a theory of freedom.

structure.title: Clauses 12–48 · Money, courts and the king's officers
structure.text: Rules about levies, fines, evidence and official requisitions make a complaint about arbitrary government unusually tangible. For the owner of a cart or a stock of corn, the limits on an officer's power can be measured in goods that remain in the yard.

structure.title: Clauses 49–63 · Redress and enforcement · What if the king breaks his word?
structure.text: The closing settlement deals with losses, hostages and the means of securing performance. Twenty-five barons are given a role in enforcing the promises, an extraordinary admission that the royal seal alone cannot settle the question of trust.

people.name: King John
people.role: The speaker granting constraints upon his own officials
people.text: The charter speaks in the ruler's voice even where it records concessions wrested from him. A seemingly gracious grant can therefore also be evidence of exactly where his government had come under pressure.

people.name: The free man
people.role: A beneficiary whose legal status matters
people.text: Some of the charter's most celebrated protections name the free man. Other clauses distinguish merchants, widows, barons and villeins, a reminder that obligations and remedies were being allocated within a society of legally differentiated ranks.

context.title: This is the charter of 1215
context.text: The agreement belongs to a quarrel between a king and rebellious barons. Later reissues and interpretations gave selected clauses an enormous afterlife. The original enforcement arrangements and details about landholding restore the particular dispute those later readers inherited.

notice.text: Notice when a promise acquires a timetable or a price.
notice.why: A general undertaking can be evaded by delay or an excessive payment. The document's apparently fussy figures and deadlines often show a beneficiary trying to close precisely that escape route.

notice.text: Follow the pronouns down the chain of power.
notice.why: In one place liberties observed by the king are also to be observed by clergy and lay lords toward their own men. A baron demanding restraint from above may have an obligation to exercise it below.

opening: A king needs money and obedience. His barons have had enough of the way he obtains them. The settlement they force on John in 1215 attends to debts, inheritances, widows, courts, and the practical business of preventing royal power from swallowing other people's security. Among these particular grievances are promises that later generations would make much larger claims upon. Reading the charter reveals the narrow, contested beginnings of a powerful idea: even a ruler can be required to answer to rules he did not simply dictate.
